positions.claim: FDE is only the right model when you must sell a highly technical product to a non-technical buyer; in the other three quadrants of the what-you-sell/who-buys matrix it is the wrong fit.
An FDE function without an underlying platform of shared primitives is not an FDE function but a dev shop, and its maintenance costs will destroy the business.
Palantir has the highest ACV of any public SaaS company in the Fortune 500 at about $4M, ahead of ServiceNow at $1.2M and Workday at about $600K, with no other public SaaS company above $500K.
Design partnerships, conventionally an early-stage startup tactic, can be scaled into enterprise — this was Palantir's core bet.

The reason FDE matters now is not that the industry recognized Palantir's model was good, but that agentic platforms are inherently customizable, which puts most software companies into the technical-product/non-technical-buyer situation.
Leaving product success to the customer's own ability to implement will make it hard to sell up market or expand horizontally or vertically.
Multiple FDEs should staff a single customer project, because a single-person engagement creates a single point of failure.
The correct granularity of platform primitives is industry-dependent, not a universal design choice — some spaces tolerate 60%-prebuilt apps while others require extremely granular configuration.
The right hiring bar for an FDE is someone you would hire as a software engineer on your team and also trust in front of a customer — no separate skill profile is needed.
Foundry's app-building platform is inherently less interesting to large tech companies because they have engineers who can build whatever apps they need in-house.
Selling technology alone fails with enterprise buyers because organized data does not by itself answer what it does for the business.
Software engineers are among the last people who should be customer-facing, which is what makes the FDE idea counterintuitive.
